passages.happening:
Rehoboam gathers 180,000 warriors from Judah and Benjamin to win the kingdom back (verse 1). But the word of the LORD comes to Shemaiah the man of God: ‘You are not to go up and fight against your brothers. Each of you must return home, for this word is from Me’ (verse 4). ‘So they listened to the words of the LORD and turned back from going against Jeroboam’ (verse 4).

‘Rehoboam continued to live in Jerusalem, and he built up cities for defense in Judah’ (verse 5): Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Hebron, Lachish, Azekah and others, with commanders, food, oil, wine, shields and spears in each (verses 6-12).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 told the split. This chapter shows the first years of the smaller kingdom going surprisingly well: Rehoboam listens to a prophet, builds defenses, and receives a stream of people from the north who want to worship at his temple. The good years are real but brief. Rehoboam reigned seventeen years, commonly dated about 931 to 913 BC, though scholars differ by a few years.

First Kings 12 tells of Shemaiah stopping the war, but the list of fortresses and the migration of priests and Levites are found only in Chronicles. The fifteen cities form a screen along Judah's eastern, southern and western approaches: the hill country, the south, the western foothills called the Shephelah, and the valleys climbing from the coast. The northern border with Israel is not fortified. Scholars debate whether the list reflects Rehoboam's reign or partly later building, and some link it with the Egyptian threat that arrives in the next chapter.

The key verb is strengthen, chazaq. It opens the middle of the chapter with the fortified cities and closes it with the faithful migrants who strengthened the kingdom. The Chronicler sets faithfulness beside military preparation as the real source of Judah's security.
passages.later: First Kings tells the same word: ‘You are not to go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites. Each of you must return home, for this word is from Me’ (1 Kings 12:24).
passages.asks: Rehoboam had an army ready, and he turned back because God said the northerners were his brothers. Ask whom you have been ready to fight who is your brother or sister. And ask what it would take for you to listen and turn back.

passages.t: The faithful come south, and Rehoboam's household
passages.happening:
The priests and Levites throughout Israel side with Rehoboam. ‘For the Levites left their pasturelands and their possessions and went to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them as priests of the LORD’ (verse 14). Jeroboam appoints his own priests ‘for the high places and for the goat demons and calf idols he had made’ (verse 15). ‘Those from every tribe of Israel who had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God followed the Levites to Jerusalem’ (verse 16), and they strengthen Judah ‘because they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon’ (verse 17).

Rehoboam marries Mahalath and Maacah daughter of Absalom, whom he loves most; ‘In all, he had eighteen wives and sixty concubines’ (verse 21). He makes Maacah's son Abijah chief among his brothers (verse 22), ‘Rehoboam also acted wisely by dispersing some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Priests and Levites did not farm tribal land; they lived in assigned towns with pasturelands and served at the sanctuary. When Jeroboam set up shrines at Dan and Bethel with golden calves and appointed priests who were not Levites, the northern Levites lost their calling, and leaving their pasturelands meant leaving their livelihood. The Chronicler adds goat demons, sa'ir, to the calves, a term the law uses for false sacrifice in the wilderness. Set their hearts to seek the LORD introduces one of the book's central ideas; the Chronicler uses two verbs for seeking, baqash and darash, as a summary of true religion.

Royal marriages built alliances, and many sons secured a dynasty. Sending sons to govern fortified cities kept them busy and loyal and spread royal authority. Who to notice: Maacah daughter of Absalom, David's rebel son, and her son Abijah, who will reign next.
passages.later: Leviticus says, ‘They must no longer offer their sacrifices to the goat demons to which they have prostituted themselves’ (Leviticus 17:7).
passages.hard:
Why does the Chronicler call Rehoboam wise in his household when the law warned kings against many wives?

Verse 23 praises Rehoboam's shrewd dispersal of his sons, not the number of his wives; the word wise there means political good sense. The Chronicler reports eighteen wives and sixty concubines without comment, and readers who knew the law for kings and the story of Solomon's wives would draw their own conclusions. Some interpreters think the Chronicler counts a large family as a sign of good in a king's faithful years, as he does with other kings. Others think the list is quietly ominous, since the next verse reports that Rehoboam abandoned the law once he was strong. Both readings take the text seriously, and the Chronicler leaves the tension for the reader to feel.
passages.asks: The Levites gave up their land and their homes to stay faithful to God's worship. Ask what faithfulness has cost you, or might. And ask what you would leave behind to be where God is truly worshiped.
